essays.stem: Describe the main records kept by a housekeeping department, and say what each one is used for.
essays.modelAnswer: The room status report shows whether each room is occupied or vacant and clean or dirty, so front office can give clean rooms to arriving guests. Room attendants' worksheets show the rooms each attendant must clean and any special requests. The logbook passes messages and unfinished jobs from one shift to the next. The lost and found register records items left by guests, so they can be stored safely and returned. The key control log shows who has each key and when it was returned, which protects guests' rooms. Maintenance requests (work orders) report faults to the maintenance team and are followed up until fixed. Linen and supplies records track stock, issues and losses. Inspection checklists record that rooms meet the standard. Accident and incident reports record what happened if someone is hurt or property is damaged.
markingPoints: Room status report and its use
Worksheets and the logbook
Lost and found register and key control log
Maintenance requests and stock (linen, supplies) records
Inspection checklists or accident reports, each with a correct use

essays.stem: Explain how to make entries in paper and electronic housekeeping records so that they are accurate, clear and complete.
essays.modelAnswer: On paper, I use the property's current form or book and write clearly in pen, never pencil, so the entry cannot be rubbed out. I fill in every box, including the date, the time and the room number, and sign or initial it. I write facts, not guesses, in short, plain sentences. If I make a mistake, I draw one line through it so it can still be read, write the correct entry next to it and initial it; I never use correction fluid or tear out pages. On the computer or phone app, I log in with my own password, select the correct room or record, type carefully, check the entry before I save it, and log off or lock the screen when I leave. In both cases I make the entry at the time, not hours later, and tell my supervisor if I find a mistake in an earlier record.
markingPoints: Uses the correct form or system; writes clearly in pen
Completes all details: date, time, room and signature
Corrects paper mistakes with one line and initials; no correction fluid
Electronic: own login, check before saving, log off
Records at the time and reports earlier mistakes

essays.stem: Explain what room status discrepancies are, including sleepers and skippers, and how housekeeping and front office deal with them.
essays.modelAnswer: A discrepancy is a difference between the room status in the housekeeping report and the status in the front office system. A sleeper is a room that front office shows as occupied, but housekeeping finds empty, with no luggage and the bed not used; often the guest has left but was not checked out, so the room cannot be sold. A skipper is a guest who has left with his luggage without paying the bill. Housekeeping prepares its room report from the attendants' checks and sends it to the front desk at set times. The two lists are compared. Every difference is rechecked: the supervisor or attendant visits the room again and front office checks the guest's account. Skippers are reported to the manager and security. Once the cause is found, both records are corrected so that rooms can be sold and the bills are right.
markingPoints: Discrepancy: difference between housekeeping and front office status
Sleeper explained correctly
Skipper explained correctly
Reports compared; each room rechecked
Reported to the right people and both records corrected

essays.stem: Describe how lost and found items are recorded, stored and returned to guests.
essays.modelAnswer: When an attendant finds an item, she hands it to the supervisor or housekeeping office straight away, without opening bags or wallets on her own. The item is recorded in the lost and found register with the date, time, room or place, the finder's name and a careful description that does not guess its value, for example "yellow metal ring" or "black phone". It is given a number, labelled or bagged with that number, and stored in a locked cupboard or safe; valuables and cash are counted in front of a witness. When a guest asks about a lost item, they must describe it and prove who they are before they are told it has been found. When it is returned, the guest signs for it and the register is updated with the date and how it was returned. Unclaimed items are kept for the period the property's policy says, then dealt with as that policy says.
markingPoints: Handed in at once; not searched alone
Register entry: date, time, place, finder, careful description
Numbered, labelled and stored locked; valuables witnessed
Guest describes the item and proves identity; signs on return
Register updated; unclaimed items dealt with by policy

essays.stem: Explain how key control records help keep guests and property safe, and what to do if a key is lost.
essays.modelAnswer: Keys, especially master and floor keys, open many rooms, so they must always be traced. The key control log records who took each key, the date and time it was issued, and when it was returned, with a signature each time. This means the property always knows who had access to a room at a given time, which helps to prevent theft and to investigate if something goes missing. Staff should keep keys on them, never lend them, never leave them in doors or on trolleys, and sign them back in at the end of the shift. Electronic key cards are also logged. If a key is lost, the staff member must report it at once to the supervisor and security, and record it. Security may change the locks or cancel and reprogramme key cards, so the lost key cannot be used.
markingPoints: Keys open many rooms, so they must be traced
Log records who, when issued and when returned, with signatures
Helps prevent and investigate theft
Good practice: keep keys on you, never lend or leave them
Lost key: report at once, record it, locks changed or cards cancelled

essays.stem: Explain how guest and staff information in housekeeping records must be kept confidential, both on paper and on computers.
essays.modelAnswer: Housekeeping records hold personal information, such as guests' names, room numbers, requests, health needs and lost property, and staff details. The data protection law and the property's rules protect this information, and guests trust the property to keep it private. On paper, worksheets and reports are kept with me or in the office, never left on trolleys or counters, and files are kept in locked cabinets. I never read out a guest's name or room number where others can hear, and I refer any visitor's questions to the front desk. Old records are shredded, not thrown in the bin. On computers and phones, I use my own password and never share it, lock the screen when I step away, and only look at the records I need for my job. I do not photograph or send guest information on my personal phone or social media.
markingPoints: Records hold personal information protected by law and the rules
Paper: kept with staff or locked away; never left on trolleys
Never reveal guest names or rooms; refer questions to the front desk
Old records shredded
Electronic: own password, lock screen, need-to-know, no personal phones or social media

essays.stem: Compare manual (paper) and electronic records systems in housekeeping, giving the advantages and disadvantages of each.
essays.modelAnswer: A manual system uses forms, books, cards and whiteboards. It is cheap, easy to learn, works when the power or internet is down, and paper with a signature is clear proof. However, it is slow to search and copy, can only be in one place at a time, can be lost or damaged by water or fire, takes up storage space, and handwriting can be hard to read. An electronic system, such as a property management system or a housekeeping app on phones, updates room status at once so front office can sell rooms quickly. It is easy to search, sort and print reports, and records can be backed up. Its disadvantages are the cost of equipment and training, the need for power and internet, and the risk of data being lost or seen by others if passwords and backups are not managed well. Many properties use both, with paper as a back-up.
markingPoints: Manual: cheap, simple, works without power
Manual: slow to search, easily lost or damaged, hard to read
Electronic: instant updates, easy to search, sort and back up
Electronic: cost, training, power and internet, security risks
Notes that properties often combine both, or a clear comparison

essays.stem: Describe the main filing methods, and explain how you would keep a filing system in good order, including archiving and disposal.
essays.modelAnswer: Alphabetical filing puts records in A to Z order, for example guest history cards by surname. Numerical filing uses numbers, such as maintenance records by room number. Chronological filing uses date order, which suits lost and found forms and logbooks. Filing by subject groups records by topic, such as suppliers, staff or chemicals. To keep the system in good order, every file is clearly labelled, papers are filed promptly in the right place, and files are put back straight after use. An index or list shows where everything is, and cabinets with guest information are locked. Records are kept for the time the property's policy or the law says. After a set time, old records that must still be kept are moved to the archive, labelled with the dates. When records are no longer needed, those with personal information are shredded or destroyed securely, as the rules say.
markingPoints: Alphabetical and numerical filing explained with examples
Chronological or subject filing explained with examples
Clear labels, prompt filing and files returned after use
Locked storage and an index
Archiving by policy, and secure destruction (shredding)

essays.stem: Explain how maintenance requests are recorded and followed up until the work is done.
essays.modelAnswer: When an attendant finds a fault, such as a dripping tap, a broken lamp or a faulty air conditioner, she reports it to the supervisor and a maintenance request (work order) is completed on paper or in the system. It records the date and time, the room or area, a clear description of the fault, how urgent it is, and who reported it. Urgent safety faults, such as water near electrics, are also phoned through at once and the room may be blocked from sale. A copy or reference number is kept by housekeeping. The maintenance team signs when they receive it and records when the work is done. Housekeeping checks the open requests each day, follows up any that are late, and checks the work once it is done. Then the request is closed in the records, and the room status is updated so the room can be sold again.
markingPoints: Fault reported and a request completed on paper or system
Details: date, location, clear description, urgency, reporter
Urgent faults phoned through; room blocked if unsafe
Copy or number kept; open requests checked and followed up
Work checked, request closed and room status updated

essays.stem: Explain why staff must follow the property's current records systems, and how they can suggest improvements.
essays.modelAnswer: Everyone must use the same current forms and systems so that records are complete, consistent and easy to find. If one attendant uses her own notebook or an old form, information is missed, rooms may be shown wrongly, lost items or keys may not be traced, and the property may not be able to prove what happened for insurance or the law. The current system has also been set up to protect guests' privacy and to link with other departments, such as front office and maintenance. Staff should be trained in the system and ask if they are unsure. If someone sees a problem, such as a form that never asks for an important detail or a step that wastes time, they should not change the system on their own. They should write the idea down with an example and suggest it to the supervisor or at a team meeting, so it can be agreed, tested and taught to everyone.
markingPoints: Common systems keep records complete, consistent and easy to find
Personal or old systems cause missed information and errors
Supports privacy, links with other departments and legal proof
Staff are trained and ask when unsure
Improvements suggested to the supervisor, not made alone, then agreed and taught

practical1.title: Complete housekeeping records for a busy shift
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a set of event cards for a morning shift at a villa or small hotel, with the property's blank forms (or a spreadsheet on a computer). Events include rooms cleaned and inspected, a guest request, a found item, a key issued and returned, a fault in a room, a "Do Not Disturb" room, and a room that front office shows as occupied but the attendant finds empty. Each member is responsible for one or two records: (1) the room status report; (2) the lost and found register and item label; (3) the key control log; (4) maintenance requests; (5) the logbook handover and guest request log (in a group of four, records 4 and 5 are shared). Update your records as the assessor calls out each event. At the end, compare the room status report with the front office list the assessor gives you, find the discrepancies and write how each will be followed up. Each member then hands over their record to another member, explaining it. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and records to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Event cards and a front office room list (from the assessor)
Blank room status report, lost and found register, key log, maintenance request forms, logbook and guest request log
Item labels and bags for found items (mock items)
A computer with a spreadsheet, if the Centre uses one
photos: The blank forms set out at the start
The found item, bagged and labelled to match the register
The room status report beside the front office list, with discrepancies marked
The written follow-up for each discrepancy
checklist: Completed their record with date, time, room and signature
Wrote clearly and corrected any mistake with a single line and initials
Described found items carefully without guessing value
Found the room status discrepancies and gave the right follow-up
Kept guest details private during the task
Explained their record clearly at handover
Used the property's forms as given, not their own notes
safety: Use made-up guest names and details only
Keep forms on the table, not where others can read them
Treat mock valuables as real: count them with a witness
Sit comfortably and keep cables and bags out of walkways

practical2.title: Set up and maintain a housekeeping filing system and electronic log
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a box of mixed, made-up housekeeping records: lost and found forms, maintenance requests, guest history cards, linen counts, staff rotas and some old records past their keeping date. As a group: (1) agree a filing system and write an index sheet; (2) sort and file the records into labelled folders or a cabinet, using alphabetical, numerical and chronological order where each suits; (3) pick out the records that are past their keeping date and mark which go to the archive and which to the (mock) shredder; (4) enter ten lost and found records into a spreadsheet on a computer, with a column for each detail, sort it by date and by room, and save a backup copy; and (5) find three records the assessor asks for, timing how long it takes. Each member leads one step and every member enters at least two records on the computer. Photograph each stage below, including the computer screen at each step, and add the photos and index to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A box of made-up housekeeping records (from the assessor)
Folders, dividers, labels and a filing box or cabinet
A computer with spreadsheet software and a USB stick or shared drive for the backup
photos: The labelled folders with records filed
The archive and shredding piles, labelled
The spreadsheet on screen, sorted by date and then by room
checklist: Helped agree a clear filing system and index
Filed records in the right order and folder
Picked out old records correctly for archive or shredding
Entered records accurately in the spreadsheet
Sorted the spreadsheet and saved a backup
Kept personal details private and logged off the computer
safety: Use only made-up records; never bring in real guest information
Lock the screen or log off when leaving the computer
Lift boxes of files with bent knees, or share the load
Keep cables tidy and out of walkways
